extracted.intended_audience: candidates preparing the French agrégation de mathématiques (oral leçon)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and syllabus-style requirements for preparing and delivering an oral 'leçon' for the French agrégation in mathematics, covering geometry, combinatorics, analysis, topology and functional spaces. Focuses on which definitions, theorems, methods, examples and applications the jury expects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Give precise definitions and canonical decompositions
rubrics_metrics.description: Present precise definitions (e.g. affine space, affine map, isometry, PGL, Lp, Sobolev spaces) and canonical decompositions (e.g. decomposition of an isometry into a translation and a vector isometry, polar decomposition).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include the definition, linear part, compatibility with inverse, injection into GL, and canonical forms when relevant (Audin, Mercier references). For groups: define group structures and important morphisms (e.g. f ↦ ~f is an isomorphism).

rubrics_metrics.name: Include illustrative examples and classifications
rubrics_metrics.description: Give concrete examples and classification results (e.g. translations, symmetries, reflections, classification of isometries in dimensions 1–3, finite subgroups of SO3, isometry groups of Platonic solids).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use tables and drawings (put diagrams in an annex) to summarize classifications (Combes, Mercier, Ulmer). For low-dimensional classification go quickly if off-topic but provide key examples and the usual tables indicating fixed-point sets or dimensions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use diagrams and annex drawings for geometry
rubrics_metrics.description: Support geometric statements (Thales, Pappus, Desargues, symmetries, tilings, conics) with drawings and place detailed figures in an annex.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The syllabus repeatedly recommends 'dessins en annexe' for planar theorems, circle/spiral illustrations, tilings (groupes paveurs) and conic classification—these improve clarity and oral exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasize methods, not only theorems
rubrics_metrics.description: In lessons (e.g. combinatorics) prefer presenting methods of resolution rather than merely listing theorems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicit injunction: 'Il faut des MÉTHODES dans cette leçon, pas seulement des théorèmes !' Give combinatorial techniques (double counting, generating functions, factor method, sieving) and show how to apply them with examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compute objects in multiple ways to provide a red thread
rubrics_metrics.description: For concrete computations (e.g. binomial coefficients, counting problems) present several different computations to maintain a coherent pedagogical thread.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example given: prove the binomial formula in two ways (multiplicative counting and induction); compute an object by derivation of power series, double counting, and algebraic manipulation to 'avoir un fil rouge'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepare to answer the 'Questions' listed for each lesson
rubrics_metrics.description: Be ready to solve and discuss the sample questions provided for each lesson topic (they indicate typical oral exam prompts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The document lists many explicit questions (e.g. inverse of Pascal matrix, why a^q = a in F_q, cardinal of GL(n,q), density questions). Candidates should prepare full solutions and be able to discuss variants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Present combinatorics topics with concrete counting tools
rubrics_metrics.description: Teach combinatorics through explicit tools: sieve formula, partitions, arrangements/permutations, combinations, binomial identities, derangements, factor method, generating functions and Burnside/orbit counting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include Dirichlet series where relevant, examples (alphabet braille, ordered samples with replacement), the formula of Burnside, orbit-count formulas, and applications (colorings, Sudoku grids, polynomials over F_q).

rubrics_metrics.name: When using groups, give group-action applications to counting
rubrics_metrics.description: Use group actions to count orbits and compute cardinals; present orbit–stabilizer and Burnside-style formulas and apply them (e.g. |P^n(F_q)|, |GL(n,q)|).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State the orbit cardinality formula |G.x| = |G|/|G_x| and the orbit-count formula |X/G| = (1/|G|) Σ_{g∈G} |X^g|. Apply to matrices, colorings, necklaces, cube colorings, and invariant objects under rotations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include standard references and suggest bibliography
rubrics_metrics.description: Cite canonical textbooks and notes for the topic (e.g. Audin, Mercier, De Biasi, Brézis, Hirsch-Lacombe, Queffelec, etc.) so examiners see the candidate's sources and the lesson's grounding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The syllabus appends tailored references per section; candidates should be familiar with at least some recommended texts and can mention them briefly in the oral.

rubrics_metrics.name: For function-space lessons, present definitions, properties and key theorems
rubrics_metrics.description: Define C^k(X), Schwartz space, holomorphic function spaces, L^p spaces, and Sobolev spaces; explain structure results (Banach/Hilbert), inclusions, density, duals, reflexivity and separability where appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cover Hölder and Minkowski inequalities, dominated convergence, Riesz-Fischer, Riesz representation (L^p duals), density of C_c^∞ in L^p (p<∞), and note special cases L^1 and L^∞. For L^2 emphasize Hilbert structure and projection theorem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discuss convolution and approximation identities in L^p
rubrics_metrics.description: Define convolution on L^p, state Young's inequality, describe approximation of the identity and use of convolutions for regularization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain that (L^1,*,·) is a commutative K-algebra without unit, dirac is not in L^1, and convolution with mollifiers yields density/regularization results and approximation properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Present Sobolev space basics and PDE existence via Lax–Milgram
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce H^1 (product, separability), continuous embeddings into C, weak/strong solutions for the Laplacian and application of Lax–Milgram to existence and uniqueness; state Poincaré inequality and boundary properties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize formulation of boundary conditions, uniqueness of weak solution implying strong solution, and give examples/applications (Dirichlet problems).

rubrics_metrics.name: For density lessons, use duality and examples from several contexts
rubrics_metrics.description: Characterize density (in metric/Banach/Hilbert contexts) and use duality arguments when orthogonality-based criteria are unavailable; provide multiple examples (polynomials dense in C^0, trigonometric polynomials, polynomials orthogonal in L^2...).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include the proof technique: if a continuous linear functional vanishes on a dense subset it vanishes everywhere. Use examples like Vandermonde-type spans, Fourier series density, and dense families from probability (iid samples).

rubrics_metrics.name: On compactness, be synthetic and include classical applications
rubrics_metrics.description: Give a concise, synthetic presentation of compactness (Heine–Borel, Borel–Lebesgue, sequential compactness, precompact+complete) and showcase key applications such as Heine theorem, Rolle, Stone–Weierstrass, fixed-point theorems and extreme value results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rapport du jury: 'Il est important de ne pas concentrer la leçon sur la compacité générale... on attend une présentation synthétique.' Include Stone–Weierstrass (separating algebras), Ascoli, Dini, and notable applications (Mercer, PDE existence, operator kernels).

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat operators compact and spectral properties for advanced candidates
rubrics_metrics.description: Define compact operators, give examples (integral operators with continuous kernel, finite-rank operators), state the spectral theorem/results on spectrum for compact operators and connections to Hilbert spaces.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mention Riesz theorem reformulations, finite-rank approximations, and use examples to illustrate spectral consequences; this is suggested for ambitious candidates in the compacity lesson.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain connectivity with emphasis on local-to-global implications
rubrics_metrics.description: Clarify definitions of connectedness and path-connectedness, stability properties, components, and the role of connectivity in passing from local to global results (e.g. uniqueness results, extension theorems).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish clearly between connectedness and path-connectedness, give examples where they differ, and present natural results using connectivity (e.g. proofs of fundamental theorems like d'Alembert–Gauss using analytic continuation, consequences for matrix groups GL(n,R)/GL(n,C)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Master completeness and its role in existence theorems
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain Cauchy sequences, complete spaces, and highlight that completeness is essential for existence theorems in infinite-dimensional spaces (e.g. Cauchy–Lipschitz, Banach fixed-point), and stress mastery of uniform convergence techniques.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rapport du jury warns: candidates should show that completeness provides existence results in function spaces and must control the Cauchy–Lipschitz theorem and uniform convergence; mention examples like L^p spaces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow jury's explicit expectations and avoid common candidate errors
rubrics_metrics.description: Heed the Jury's remarks: avoid over-concentrating on tangential generalities (e.g. general compactness theory without applications), ensure key proofs are known and include illustrative applications, and do not omit basic expected material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of jury guidance in the text: prefer synthetic presentation, include examples of operators with continuous kernels, Montel/families of holomorphic functions for ambitious candidates, and be prepared to demonstrate standard theorems (Heine, Rolle, Stone–Weierstrass, Cauchy-Lipschitz).
